# Question Design Basics

## What a stem is

The stem is the part of a multiple-choice item that poses the problem. A good
stem can be answered by a knowledgeable candidate without reading the options
at all. If the stem cannot stand alone, the item is testing reading speed
rather than the subject.

## Rules that survive contact with real candidates

1. Put the question in the stem, not in the options. "Which of the following
   is NOT..." forces the candidate to hold four negations at once.
2. Keep the options parallel in length and grammar. The longest option is
   correct far more often than chance in hand-written banks, and test-wise
   candidates know it.
3. Avoid "all of the above". A candidate who recognises two correct options
   can select it without evaluating the third.
4. One defensible answer. If two options are arguably correct, the item will
   be challenged and the challenge will be upheld.

## Distractors

A distractor exists to be chosen by a candidate who holds a specific
misconception. A distractor that nobody selects is dead weight: it makes the
item a three-option question with four options' worth of reading. Review
selection frequencies after every sitting and replace anything below five per
cent.

## Difficulty

Difficulty is a property of the item and the cohort together, not of the item
alone. An item with a facility value above 0.95 discriminates nothing. One
below 0.20 is usually broken rather than hard.

<<<END DOCUMENT>>>

<<<DOCUMENT corpus/02_assessment_integrity.txt>>>
ASSESSMENT INTEGRITY IN UNPROCTORED EXAMINATIONS
Internal guidance note, revision 4

1. THE PROBLEM

An unproctored examination cannot prevent collusion. It can only make
collusion expensive, detectable, or pointless. Controls that assume the
candidate is alone in a room are not controls; they are hopes.

2. CONTROLS THAT WORK

Item banking at scale. If every candidate receives a different set of
questions drawn from a large bank, the value of sharing answers falls sharply.
The bank must be large enough that overlap between any two candidates is low,
which in practice means several hundred items per topic.

Time pressure applied honestly. A tight window reduces the opportunity to
consult, but it also penalises slow readers who know the material. Use it
sparingly and state it in advance.

Question rotation. Items that have been sitting in a bank for three years are
in circulation. Treat an item's age as a risk factor.

3. CONTROLS THAT DO NOT WORK

Honour statements. Measurable effect close to zero in every published study.

Browser lockdown on a personal device. Defeated by a second device.

Webcam monitoring without a human watching. Produces evidence after the fact,
not prevention, and generates a volume of flags nobody reviews.

4. WHAT TO RECORD

Every item's exposure count. Every challenge and its outcome. Every change to
the bank, with a date and a reason.

<<<END DOCUMENT>>>

<<<DOCUMENT corpus/03_item_writing_guidelines.pdf>>>
Item Writing Guidelines
Examinations Office — standing guidance for subject leads. Revision 7, September 2026.
1. Before you write
Agree the blueprint first. A blueprint states how many items each topic receives and at which
cognitive level. Writing items before the blueprint exists produces a bank that is dense where
writing was easy and empty where it was not.
Every item must trace to a syllabus outcome. An item that traces to nothing is unmarkable in a
challenge, because there is no agreed standard to measure the candidate's answer against.
2. While you write
Write the correct answer first, then the distractors. Writing distractors first produces items where
the correct option is the one that reads most carefully.
Each distractor should correspond to a named misconception. Record the misconception alongside
the item. When the item is reviewed in two years, that note is the only thing that explains why the
distractor is there.
Keep numeric options in order. A candidate scanning an unordered numeric list is doing arithmetic
on the layout.
3. Review
Two reviewers, one of whom did not write the item. The writer cannot see their own ambiguity; that
is what makes it ambiguity rather than a mistake.
Review for accessibility at the same time. An item that depends on colour, on a figure with no
alternative text, or on a cultural reference is measuring something other than the outcome.
4. After the sitting
Compute facility and discrimination for every item. Retire items with negative discrimination
immediately: a negative value means stronger candidates chose a distractor, which is evidence the
key is wrong or the stem is misleading.
Record the exposure count. Items are a depleting resource and a bank with no exposure tracking
has no idea which of its items are already in circulation.

<<<END DOCUMENT>>>

<<<DOCUMENT corpus/04_academic_integrity_deck.pptx>>>
[slide 1]
Academic Integrity in Online Assessment
Staff development session — Examinations Office, September 2026
[slide 2]
What we are actually defending
The mark has to mean something.
A qualification is a claim the institution makes about a person.
Every uncontrolled sitting weakens that claim a little.
The question is never whether cheating is possible. It is what it costs.
[speaker notes] Open by asking the room how many of their items are more than three years old. Usually most hands stay down, which is the point.
[slide 3]
Three things that do not work
Honour statements: measurable effect close to zero.
Browser lockdown on a personal device: defeated by a second device.
Webcam flags nobody reviews: evidence after the fact, not prevention.
All three are popular because they are visible, not because they work.
[speaker notes] Do not spend long here. The room already suspects this and labouring it makes the session feel like a complaint.
[slide 4]
What does work
A bank large enough that two candidates overlap very little.
Rotation, with item age treated as a risk factor.
Exposure counts recorded for every item.
Challenge outcomes fed back into the bank.
[slide 5]
Generated items
A language model can draft items quickly.
It cannot tell you which outcome an item traces to.
Review by a subject lead is not optional, and it is the slow part.
Budget the review time before you budget the generation time.
[speaker notes] This is the slide people quote back afterwards. Leave it up while taking questions.
[slide 6]
What to take away
Bank size is a budget line.
Exposure tracking is the cheapest control you are not using.
Review capacity, not generation capacity, is the real constraint.
[speaker notes] Close on the review-capacity point and stop.
<<<END DOCUMENT>>>

<<<DOCUMENT corpus/05_bloom_taxonomy_notes.md>>>
# Bloom's Taxonomy and Question Levels

## The six levels, revised

Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. The revised taxonomy
uses verbs rather than nouns, which matters when writing items because the verb
in the stem is what fixes the level.

## Mapping verbs to levels

| Level | Verbs that usually indicate it |
|---|---|
| Remember | define, list, name, state |
| Understand | explain, summarise, classify |
| Apply | compute, solve, demonstrate, use |
| Analyse | compare, distinguish, attribute |
| Evaluate | justify, critique, defend, judge |
| Create | design, construct, formulate |

## The common failure

Most hand-written banks cluster at Remember and Understand, because those items
are quick to write and quick to mark. A bank with eighty per cent recall items
tests preparation rather than competence.

A question that asks a candidate to justify a design choice sits at Evaluate,
not at Understand, even when the underlying fact is trivial. The level is set
by what the candidate must do, not by how hard the content is.

## Writing above Apply

Items above Apply usually need a scenario. The scenario costs words and the
marking costs time, which is why banks drift downward under deadline pressure.
Budget for it explicitly or it will not happen.

<<<END DOCUMENT>>>

<<<DOCUMENT corpus/06_exam_security_handbook.pdf>>>
Examination Security Handbook
Examinations Office — handbook for online delivery. Revision 2, downloaded September 2026.
1. Scope
This handbook covers the delivery of summative assessment outside a supervised hall. It does not
cover coursework, portfolios or oral examinations, each of which has its own guidance.
2. Candidate authentication
Authentication establishes that the person sitting the paper holds the account. It does not establish
that the person is working alone, and no amount of authentication will. Treat the two problems
separately or you will buy a solution to the wrong one.
Single sign-on through the institutional identity provider is the baseline. Where a second factor is
available, require it for the sitting itself and not only for the login.
3. Item exposure
Every item that is shown to a candidate is potentially public from that moment. Plan on the
assumption that it is. The cost of an exposed item is the cost of writing its replacement, which is
why bank size is a budget line and not a technical detail.
4. Automated generation
Where items are produced with the assistance of a language model, the generated text must be
reviewed by a subject lead before it enters the bank. Generated items carry the same traceability
requirement as hand-written ones.
5. Incident handling
Record every suspected breach with a timestamp, the items involved and the action taken. A
breach register with no entries is more often evidence of a missing process than of a secure one.
Retire exposed items rather than rewriting them in place. A rewritten item keeps its identifier and its
exposure history follows it, which corrupts the statistics for everything that depends on them.

<<<END DOCUMENT>>>

function.name: topic_lookup
function.description: Search the client's approved topic list by topic name. Use it to check which topics the client allows before writing questions. Pass a word or phrase from a topic name, for example 'bloom' or 'distractor'. Returns up to `limit` matches, each with an id and a name. It searches topic names only. It does not read files and does not take a path.

parameters.description: Arguments for topic_lookup. There is no filename here, on purpose.

query.description: A word or phrase to match against the client's approved topic names. Case-insensitive.
query.title: Query

limit.description: How many matching topics to return at most.
limit.title: Limit

parameters.title: TopicLookupArgs

function.name: question_lookup
function.description: Search the questions that have already been generated and stored. Use it before writing a question, to check whether a similar one already exists, so that you do not repeat it. Pass a word or phrase from the question or its topic. Returns up to `limit` matches, each with an id, topic, text and source. It does not read files and does not take a path.

query.description: Text to match against questions already generated.
query.title: Query

limit.description: How many matches to return at most.
limit.title: Limit
